utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Jovan Simic, can we hear what is happening to Mr. Kvocka. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I approach the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Prcac is suffering terrible pain. He's been suffering from 5.00 this morning. He can't see very well. He has very severe headaches. He has taken his medication but it doesn't seem to have helped. If you agree, we agree that the trial continue without him, and we could contact the Registry to call in a physician. I think that would be the right way to continue. Perhaps he could have a rest, if that is agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, is there anything you can do by way of assistance? Can we call the nurse or a doctor, perhaps, to help Mr. Prcac?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can call the nurse and see if she could see him right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Jovan Simic, we agree that Mr. Prcac be allowed to leave the courtroom and receive medical assistance. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one more point. May I accompany Mr. Prcac, at least to begin with, for purposes of communication. Perhaps I could help him communicate with the nurse. And I would return later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Masic is in the courtroom so we can go ahead. You have permission to leave. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to resume the proceedings with the testimony of the witness who testified yesterday, and it is not the cross-examination yet. We have redirect by Mr. Krstan Simic, and I can see Mr. Stojanovic on his feet. Would you have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. Just one moment, please, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for giving me the floor. Having consulted my colleagues, the Defence of Zigic will not be asking any questions. So I would just like to inform you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been given the opportunity, though. Mr. Usher, please have the witness shown in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bolta. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Let me remind you that you are continuing your testimony under oath and you are going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Perhaps you could approach the microphone. That's right. Mr. Krstan Simic, you have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning to you too, Mr. Bolta.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you yesterday during his cross-examination the following, he said: Did you and your colleagues, Tomo Stojakovic, the reservist whose name I forgot, opened the windows to the door of the Black Meraja van, that is to say, the part envisaged for the transport of persons taken into custody, the prisoners? The official vehicle, in that portion, are there any windows at all and can they be opened?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no windows and therefore no windows can be opened in that part of the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, in the official vehicle that we refer to as Black Meraja, how is the question of ventilation regulated for persons being transported and who are in that particular section of the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was regulated by the manufacturers, by the factory, and has a system of ventilation. And that is why we refer to it as the Black Meraja. It is a special vehicle where ventilation has been incorporated into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Once again, would you please make pauses between question and answer, and perhaps you could take a look at the screen to see when the court reporters and the interpreters have finished. You were also asked whether you gave any water to the persons transported from Keraterm to Omarska. And so I would like to ask you two questions now. The first is: How far is Keraterm from Omarska? And the second question: How long does it take to drive this distance from Keraterm to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance between Keraterm to Omarska is about 25 kilometres. And the route to Omarska, and the time it takes to reach Omarska is between 25 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you made these two transports from the police station to Omarska, did you stop anywhere else except Keraterm? Did you stop in front of a cafe and leave the detainees in the van, and you yourself leaving the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My learned colleague also asked you about the way in which the distinction between the police station and police station departments, and the standards that apply to both categories. And within that context, I'm going to ask you the following question: Who decides, who makes the decision as to where a station -- where the police force will have a station and where it will have a department? Under whose competence does that come?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is under the competence of the Ministry or, rather, the Minister for the Interior, or persons who he authorises. But usually it is the minister himself who makes decisions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My learned colleague also asked you about the first time you went, and you said that it was in mid-May and that you can't quite get your bearings, but that you are certain that it was in May, because you transported individuals whom you did not know. Now, that first transport, the first transfer you made from Keraterm, when you came from the police station to Omarska, can you link that up to some other event perhaps for you to be able to pinpoint the date? Roughly when your first arrival at Omarska took place.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you the exact date, but I know that an order was received with respect to some problems regarding the conditions in Keraterm, and the detainees had to be transferred to Omarska because of some of the conditions there. But I don't actually know what they were in Keraterm for the detainees to have to be transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, and you tell me if I have or have not, it was when the people were transferred from Keraterm to Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I asked you and you gave me a detailed description, and my learned colleague asked you again and your answer was yes to him to a particular question, and now I have one more question for you. When you were already in Omarska, when Mr. Kvocka -- from the reservist whom you do not know took the list and went to the administrative building, and when he returned with that piece of paper, what did he say in connection to Mr. Nusret Sivac?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was sitting in the vehicle, the motor was switched off, the windows were open, as far as I was able to hear, the chief said to Mr. Kvocka that Nusret Sivac -- that they didn't need Nusret Sivac, that (redacted). He was Nusret (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the chief said that they did not need Mr. Sivac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bolta.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can try to help me understand more fully certain facts you mentioned. I'll go back. When you said that you arrived at the camp, and to cut a long story short, Mr. Kvocka saw you, saw Nusret Sivac, and was surprised. And I'll mention words. He told them, "Boys, this is rough treatment," seeing that they were badly handled. Now, you said that immediately the bad treatment stopped, and not only it stopped, after Kvocka left, they did not go back to this treatment. All mistreatment did not continue after Kvocka left. Now, just, in fact, this gave you the impression that Kvocka was a man of authority in the camp? He was obeyed even after he left.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have the impression that he was a man of authority. He just warned the people that, according to the rules and regulations for public security, that searches should not be conducted in that way. And he just drew attention to that person who had a short haircut and who was tall, and he was probably their commandeer. So when that particular man gave out these orders, they did not behave in the way they had behaved up until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you could see that it was a disciplined camp, because they would take an order and obey it even after the man who gave the order went away. This was a disciplined camp or it was completely out of control, where everybody could do what he likes?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was control in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Mr. Kvocka was one of the people in control?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was, no, because he was shift leader -- patrol sector leader in the police department. So he had no competencies as a leadership cadre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. But they listened to him. What they said was obeyed, whatever he was. According to you, what you saw, you said they stopped the mistreatment and did not go back to it even after he left.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Kvocka knows how persons are frisked, he just warned the men -- warned, actually, that person who was in charge of these special forces in Omarska and told this leader that they shouldn't behave that way. So it was the leader that had the authority over the others, not Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And what authority did he have on the leader? Could he punish the leader? Why did the leader obey him? I mean, you were there, I was not there, so I wanted your opinion. If he was a leader, why did the leader obey him? Why was he almost afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was afraid of him, no. But he probably knew that Kvocka worked in the police force and that he knew the laws and the rules and regulations as regards conduct. And so he could see himself that the frisking was being done in a rough manner. He realised it himself, I suppose, this leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, he did not realise it before Kvocka came. I mean, he changed his method on the instructions of Mr. Kvocka. That's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, one thing else. You said that Mr. Delic replaced Drljaca, and you said you thought, you said exactly, "I think he proposed Kvocka as shift leader and made this proposition to the Minister." Now, that means that Mr. Kvocka was looked upon as a good policeman and was regarded favourably; is that the impression you had?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, he was not put aside -- he was put aside by Drljaca, if I understood rightly, because he was put aside by Drljaca and then Delic wanted him back. What happened after that? What happened to this proposition?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. You said that Mr. Delic proposed Kvocka as shift leader to the minister, but you didn't tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the proposal went to the minister, the minister confirmed it and Kvocka was the shift leader of the Prijedor Police Station at the end of 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he was looked upon as a very good policeman by the authorities, as a loyal policeman?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, I want to understand a little bit better the testimony that you gave about the occasions in which the bus that -- the van that you were driving stopped at the camps. Now, tell me if I'm correct, that the occasion -- two occasions when your van stopped at Omarska, you told us that you were able to see the fact that the prisoners getting out of the van were being searched in a rough way, once when Mr. Kvocka intervened and the earlier time when he wasn't there to intervene. You mentioned that you were able to see that they were treated roughly. And then additionally, on the second time, you were able to tell us about the incident where Mr. Kvocka said Mr. Nusret Sivac was the wrong person. You also told us that both times you were only stopped at the camp for about five minutes, I think you said. And then you told us, however, that on the second trip, when the van stopped at Keraterm, you were not able to see if anything was going on in back when the prisoners were put on, or you were asked if you knew anything -- you were able to see prisoners being dragged out and beaten, and you said no, you didn't know anything about that and you weren't able to see anything about prisoners in the back of the van, coming in or getting out. I'm wondering if you can help me a little to understand. If you were in the van all the time, and you told us on one occasion you could hear the conversation because the engine was off and the windows were up, how you would be able to see and hear so much during such a short time in the two times the van stopped at Omarska but you weren't able to hear or see anything about -- anything that might have been happening to the prisoners when it stopped in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I was sitting in the van. My colleague, Tomo, got off and opened the back door. The men got off and they were taken over by the reserve officer who was there. Then this special unit arrived and they searched these people, because I stopped right at the corner of the administrative building so I couldn't see the whole side of the building but only a part of it. What I could see, I could see through the window and the side window, but I couldn't see the rest of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's true. You're now talking about Omarska; right? You're now talking about when it stopped at Omarska, as opposed to when it stopped at Keraterm. What I'm just trying to understand is if you were always sitting in the van, how you were able to see so much of what was happening in Omarska but nothing of what was happening in Keraterm to the prisoners as they got out or came in. I just wanted you to clarify that, if you were in the van both times.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the van. And Tomo got off, because the persons were already prepared for transport, they were waiting for us to come, and they were simply boarded onto the van, at the back, and we continued on our way to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to finish this off, I understand you to say that you just couldn't -- is this correct, your earlier testimony: You were not in a position to see or hear anything about what was happening to the prisoners as they got onto the van in Keraterm; is that right? You were asked whether you heard any commotion, whether you knew anything happened, and you said no, you were sitting in the van and you couldn't -- I think that's what you said, you couldn't see or hear what was happening because your friend, your colleague, Mr. Stojakovic, was the one who was out with the prisoners in Keraterm as they were loaded on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing was happening in Keraterm, actually, when the people got onto the van.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to pin down now because I didn't fully understand it. Is it that you couldn't tell because you were in the front of the van and Mr. Stojakovic was out with the prisoners in back, so you couldn't tell if anything was happening; or you could see what was happening and nothing was happening? I just wanted to clarify which of those two things you are testifying to. That you could see that nothing was happening or you couldn't see whether anything was happening?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really see, because when I made an about-turn in Keraterm, I was facing the road, I was facing the way out, the road leading to Omarska. So that's all I could say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. In Keraterm, after you picked up the prisoners on this second trip, and your colleague, Mr. Stojakovic, came back into the van after the prisoners were loaded, did he say anything to you about anything unusual happening? He was the one who was out there with them as they were loaded onto the van. Did he mention anything, say anything, about anything unusual happening in the process of their being loaded onto the van?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. On either of the two trips that you made, did you -- were you able to see the condition of prisoners as they were picked up at the police station, at the police station, and put into the van? Were you in a position to see what they looked like as they came onto the van from the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are referring to the three men, plus Nusret Sivac, that I was driving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to any -- you said you made two trips -- to anybody that you picked up at the time, on either trip, from the police station into -- that came into the van. I just want to know if you could see them as they were coming onto the van.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So my next question is: Were any of those men, men or whoever they were, on either one of the trips, could you see any -- what condition were they in? Were they bruised? Was there any evidence that they had been beaten? Were they dishevelled? I mean, what condition were they in when they got onto the van from the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three, or, rather, Nusret Sivac and the two men who were in the police station, as far as I saw, they had not been beaten, nor did they have any kind of injuries, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. How about the other trip? Did you pick people up from the police station on the other trip, the first trip? The first time that you went to Keraterm and Omarska, the one that was sometime in May, did you pick people up from the police station that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was from Keraterm. We were transferring people from Keraterm to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you for straightening that out for me. When you picked them up at Keraterm, could you see them as they came onto the van? This first trip, not the Nusret Sivac time. Could you see the prisoners as they were getting onto the van in Keraterm on the very first time that you were there, in May.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You couldn't see them when they got on at Keraterm. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Bolta, I too have three questions for you. The first: When Mr. Kvocka took the list from the reserve officer to do something, he said something. Do you remember his exact words, what exactly he said?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what Mr. Kvocka said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Kvocka asked with surprise, "What are you, Nusret, doing here?" The answer was that he had been arrested and he had no idea why. Then Kvocka took the piece of paper from the reserve officer and said that he would go upstairs to see with the chiefs in the administrative building what it was all about, whether they needed Nusret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember now his words, what exactly he said? Before he left, having picked up the list and holding the list in his hand, and before leaving, what exactly did he say?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said that he would check with the chiefs what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he say "the chiefs" or "the chief," one? Singular or plural?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said the chief or the chiefs -- the chiefs or the superiors, I don't know. I think he used the plural, the chiefs. Well, I couldn't hear very clearly as I was sitting in the vehicle, so I didn't really hear whether he used a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I heard you say just now that there were several chiefs. Why are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I heard, that he said, "I'm going to see what the chiefs -- what's going on." How many chiefs there were, I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You're telling me that there were several chiefs because Mr. Kvocka said that he was going to see the chiefs, and your conclusion on the basis of that is that there were several; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I am not quite sure whether he said he was going to the chief or the chiefs. But in any event, he went to the administrative building, and when he came back, he said that they didn't need Nusret Sivac (redacted) Mr. Nusret Sivac was driven back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Another question. Nusret Sivac, this name, when was the first time that you heard that name? When did you learn that name? When did you hear of that name for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Nusret Sivac worked in the public security station in Prijedor and he worked at the telephone exchange, he worked in the communications, and when I was transferred from Zagreb, a couple of months later, I learnt about Mr. Sivac. This could have been in March or April of 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You mentioned that the way in which people were searched was rough or brutal, that is the word you used. Do you know the rules governing such procedures?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why didn't you intervene when you saw that the search was being done in a brutal manner?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to intervene at all at that point in time because I was not competent. There were people higher up than me; there were unit leaders there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You had no authority to do that. Why did Mr. Kvocka do it, then?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he happened to be there just then. He was outside and he saw that they were treating the persons roughly, and then he drew the attention of the leader of that unit to that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you were there too and you saw that the procedures were being done in a brutal manner. What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is that my orders were to transport these people, and in the police, one follows orders. Whatever orders you receive, that is what you have to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, yes. I see that Judge Fouad Riad has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. [In English] Listening to you yesterday and then listening to you now, I understood that Mr. Kvocka did two different actions; one, when he said -- you said as soon as you brought the men, he said, "Boys, this is a rough treatment," and then you continued saying a man came and stopped the bad treatment. This was an action. And then now you are telling the President that he went to the chiefs to check about Nusret Sivac. So my concern is when he said this is the bad treatment and they stopped the treatment, he did that immediately, or he went first to the chiefs and then came back this is a bad treatment because the chiefs have decided it's a bad treatment?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as he came up, he said that straight away. "Boys, that is not the way to search persons." And then he took up the piece of paper from that reserve officer and went to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the bad treatment stopped immediately when he said that.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the leader of this special unit, when Kvocka made his comment, then the leader of the unit gave orders that they should stop that treatment. So he was the one issuing the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but Kvocka did not need to go to the chiefs to get an order to stop that bad treatment. He went to the chiefs just for Nusret.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he too knew Nusret Sivac as well as all the other officers who had worked with him, and he was surprised to see him there so he went to check with the chiefs what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: About Nusret. I mean, the bad treatment had already stopped.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bolta, thank you very much for coming here. I see Mr. Simic on his feet. Before I finish what I was going to say. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to appeal to the Chamber, pursuant to the exceptions that we had in the past, to allow me to put a question linked to the question put by His Honour Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the question, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question would be the following: For the witness to state clearly whether, on that occasion, Mr. Kvocka issued an order, or was it the advice of an experienced policeman and nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw Mr. Saxon get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has testified that he did not work at the camp, that he had no specialised knowledge of the operations of the camp, that he spent a total of ten minutes at the Omarska camp during 1992, so it would be pure speculation on this witness' part to give such an opinion. And, quite frankly, this testimony has been explained thoroughly yesterday and today, so we would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, I should like to ask you kindly to tell this Trial Chamber, and you are a policeman, whether on that occasion Mr. Kvocka was giving those persons an order, or was he giving them a piece of advice as an experienced policeman, or suggestion as to how they should act, pursuant to the Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka was giving advice as to the way in which a search should be done. And as far as I remember, what he said was, "Guys, that is not the way to act, according to the rules," because they were acting in a rough manner. So he just gave them this admonition, and then of course this unit leader prevented them from continuing with that treatment. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Bolta, I have a question. [Interpretation] I'm going to switch back to French. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I heard you say or mention a member of special units here. Were there other policemen present, apart from Mr. Kvocka, or was he alone?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, I didn't see anyone except --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry. At the time that Mr. Kvocka said stop -- no, let me rephrase the question. What were the words used by Mr. Kvocka to have the search stopped? The words used by Mr. Kvocka. Don't tell me, "He said that ..." Give us the exact quote.

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Boys, that is not the way to search persons. You have to work and study in the police for a long time to be able to do your work as a policeman properly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, but we will check with the transcript, I think that the first time you said that he ordered, "Stop it," but now you're saying that that is not the proper way to carry out a search. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was just explaining how the search should be done. And the leader of the special unit was the one who issued the order. He told his men to stop it, to stop acting in that way. So the leader, the superior who was there present, this tall man with a short haircut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So were there any other persons there apart from Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was this leader that you are mentioning? You mentioned a leader of a special unit. Who was he? Was he doing the search? Was the leader doing the search?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know who he is, nor was he doing the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you mentioned, I'm looking at the transcript, page 20, line 6, when you said, "And the leader of the special unit was the one who issued the order." I'm asking you, who was that leader?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the special unit? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know the name but you knew he was the leader. How did things happen? What were the words used by the leader? What did the leader actually say?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could conclude that he was the leader of that unit, because when he came up and when Kvocka said this, he stopped the procedure from continuing in that way. So from that I concluded that he must have been the leader of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know how long this went on for?

utterances.speaker: BRANE BOLTA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Bolta. I think we have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in accordance with our plan, the Defence calls witness Novak Pusac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, how do we stand regarding the number of witnesses here present, in relation to those present here for this week? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have one further witness, so we had planned to finish today, and we believe we will manage to do that so that they won't have to come back again or for us to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pusac. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Thank you very much for coming. First, you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, good morning. And as you know, I am attorney Krstan Simic representing, together with Mr. Lukic, Mr. Kvocka. So our questions will be in that context and related to this case, of course. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, for the record, will you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Pusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: On the 5th of March, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you born? Sorry, in Prska? Is that where you reside?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm told your place of birth has not been entered in the record. So will you please make a pause. Where were you born? Where? Where?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What kind of education do you have?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I'm a mechanic, a secondary school education.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Have you done your military service?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In 1981, in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What arm of the military did you serve in in Nis

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I served as a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you completed your obligatory military service, were you a military conscript? And if you were, where were your documents?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a military -- I was a conscript, and I was registered with the military department in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, we won't discuss the events that took place in Prijedor, as Their Honours have heard about that in some detail. We should just discuss your role in those events. So my question to you is: Did you, from the military -- were you drafted in 1991 by the military authorities at the time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know what unit you were drafted to?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The 43rd Motorised Brigade, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As a member of the 43rd Motorised Brigade in Prijedor, did you take part in armed clashes in the course of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was the 43rd Motorised Brigade based?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did it have its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In May or April 1992 and later, was there a change in your military assignment, and which unit were you assigned to then?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Which unit was it?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence for Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was the Territorial Defence unit in Omarska located?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In Omarska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the commander of the Omarska Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Ranko Radenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, did you, together with a number of soldiers, at the end of May, or beginning of June, receive as a unit a definite military task?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you begin implementing that assignment that we will come back to?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: At the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was that military assignment given to this smaller unit as a component of the Omarska Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The second circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: We were in the second circle securing the area we were ordered to secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you secure the area of the Omarska complex where some persons were detained at the time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How was that security organised of this second circle, as you call it, this second ring? How far were you away from the Omarska complex where these persons were being detained?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: 500 to 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did a lower level unit within the Territorial Defence receive orders to provide that security? If there was such a unit, who was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. leader of that unit?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It was actually a company, and the leader of the company was Drago Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How was the system of shifts organised or, rather, how many hours did a shift provide security for?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: One guard post was secured by four of us, two were resting, and two were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me just check whether I understood you correctly. So that means that you and another soldier were on guard duty for 24 hours, and then another two would relieve you and you would be off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know how many such guard posts there were?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How far were the guard posts from you to the left and to the right, if you had neighbours who were also providing guard duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: About 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As you would spend the night at those guard posts, was there any form of a accommodation there or the like?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: We provided those conditions ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of tents or shelters?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, we had small tents.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean that you and your colleague, during those 24 hours, would take turns, would organise yourselves so as to take turns? One would be on duty and the other resting.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you told what the aim of this second security ring was? Did you have any instructions about that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the aim of providing this second ring of security?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: To prevent entry from the outside and escapes from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was the possibility mentioned to you of an attack by members of the Green Berets in order to free the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I would just like to ask the Chamber if, from this point where we're getting into much more contested areas than the background issues, if perhaps the chamber would consider seeking a reduction in the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really didn't notice a single leading question except for the last one, which for me is, after all, quite irrelevant, really. It's irrelevant from the standpoint of this case, because we intend to show the structure within the camp. But we're not discussing the strategy of attack or defence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, you may continue, having made that remark. So please proceed. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did this Territorial Defence unit of Omarska have in its composition a quartermaster platoon?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was its task?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Its task was to prepare and deliver food.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you aware where the quartermaster platoon was located?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In the separation -- it was separated from Omarska. It was outside Omarska. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My colleague has warned me that there is an unclear point so I'll try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How far is this separation, as it's called, Separacija, away from the complex of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: 1900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do the buildings on the location known as Separacija also belong to the iron ore mine of Ljubija? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: This quartermaster platoon, did it have in its composition soldiers from reserve forces in charge of preparing food?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were there other soldiers in charge of distributing the food?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the quartermaster platoon?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Milan Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Pero Rendic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: He organised the preparation of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did I then understand you correctly as saying that Pero Rendic was superior to this group of men who prepared the food?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What were the duties of Mr. Andzic, then?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: His duties were to provide the foodstuffs for the quartermaster platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever during your stay there visit Separacija?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The food that was prepared by the quartermaster platoon in Separacija, was it also delivered to members of the Omarska Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How many meals a day did you receive?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the food like, the food that you also received as a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It was good in terms of quantity, but it was bland. There were no spices in it and that's not the kind of food we were used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You served in the army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was there any difference between the food you ate in the army and that you ate in the field? Not in terms of taste but in terms of ingredients.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you receive -- were you given bread with that food?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How much bread?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: A quarter of a loaf, sometimes an eighth, depending on the situation in the bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, did you and the other soldiers ever object to the quality of that bread?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the substance of your objection?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It was either not well-baked or it was simply of poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did it have to do with power cuts that occurred at that time?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the greatest problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, here we are. There are several situations, but here you have a good example of a leading question. That's what I mean. Maybe you're not noticing it but we are. So please pay attention, be careful. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I accept your suggestion and I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did you, during the times when you were on duty, deal with the problem of your own nutrition?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: When we were resting, we were at home and we ate there. When we were on duty, we brought food from home.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior, your immediate superior, the first above you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Zdravko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Ranko Radenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: To you, Zdravko Maric, or any other member of the Omarska Territorial Defence unit, could Zeljko Meakic, commander of the police station, issue any orders to any of you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zeljko Meakic ever visit your guard posts?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of your Territorial Defence unit was subordinated to, I mean Mr. Ranko Radenovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Within that unit, did you have -- did you maintain discipline? Did the guards conscientiously fulfil their tasks of providing security in the second ring?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The discipline was not up to snuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In what was it reflected, this lack of discipline?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Sleeping; people went home when they were not supposed to; played card games.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you personally ever go to the Omarska camp where the detainees were?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other members of security of the second ring going to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, nobody went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And finally, did the security you provided have anything in common with the security provided by members of the police from the police station department within the compound?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we wanted to interpose an objection in that there's no basis that this individual would have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, perhaps you can ask the witness what he could observe, what he could have observed. But if the witness tells you, if I got it correctly, that he never entered into the compound of Omarska, he is not in a position to compare. So perhaps you should bear that in mind. Please continue. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to respond to Ms. Somers, and this was my last question. I had the grounds for this question because a couple of minutes earlier, I asked him whether the commander of the police station, Zeljko Meakic, could he ever give them orders. I got his answer, "No." I asked whether Zeljko Meakic had ever come to see what they were doing, and he said no. And I now asked a question which only the -- the answer to which only confirms what is written in the order of the 31st of May, 1992. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Krstan Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Thank you very much, in any case. So, Ms. Somers -- I'm sorry, is there anyone on the other Defence teams who wishes to put any questions? I see them signing no. So, Ms. Susan Somers, how much time do you need approximately for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues, I would like to ask a few questions based on his testimony, and then ask for his assistance in going through one document. So I think it would be commensurate with, perhaps, the time that was taken for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we know you are going to do this. But how much time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It will go beyond 11.00. So maybe half an hour, maybe 40 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, then. I just asked this to see if it is better to take our break now or later because if you could finish in a quarter of an hour, we could wait. In any case, we are now going to take a break of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Jovan Simic, I apologise for interrupting you, but could you bring us an update with respect to Mr. Prcac's condition. How is he feeling? Is he feeling better? Has somebody seen to him? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Prcac has been transferred to the Detention Unit and a physician is seeing him. He has a very high blood pressure, over 200, and he is experiencing severe pain in his head and neck, which has upset his eyesight too. They hope that he will be better. He will have to receive therapy for reducing his blood pressure and a prescription for his heart. I talked to him during the break and I will do so again in the coming break. He feels a little better but his situation is, nonetheless, critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. Mr. Usher, please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Pusac. You are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. Ms. Susan Somers, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, could you, before getting into any other questions, give us the exact date, day and -- I'm sorry, year, and month when you came to Omarska camp to work, and the exact date, year, and month when you left?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Do you mean did I work in the firm, in the company? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has testified but he never said that he went to work in the Omarska camp. He said that within the frameworks of his unit he was assigned the task of security. So could questions be posed in that sense, that is to say, when the unit received its assignment to provide security for the camp and not to work in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I will gladly rephrase it, Your Honour. I don't want to confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Mr. Pusac. Let me phrase that a little bit more clearly. When did you start your work as guard duty in the second circle and then when did you finish it? Month and year starting and month and year finishing, please.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I started working at the beginning of June 1992 and stopped working at the beginning of August of that same year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the commander of Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a person by the name of Dusan Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I have heard of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what connection?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Just as a name, the name of a man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understood your testimony a bit earlier. Did you indicate that you were not authorised to enter the camp proper, neither you nor your group with whom you worked on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: That's right. We weren't authorised to enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that the first ring, the first ring of the camp where the prisoners were kept, was manned by policemen; right? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness was not in the camp at all and does not know what was going on in the camp for him to be able to assert or deny the facts asked him by Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he was working in the second circle, the second ring, so the second comes after the first. Go ahead with your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, shall I repeat the question or do you remember it? Let me repeat it for you. The first ring of the camp, which was outside of where the prisoners were kept, was manned by policemen, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know which formations kept that ring.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had told us that you received, you and the guards with whom you worked in the second circle, received two meals a day, and if I understood correctly, the amount you got was okay, it was just not to your taste. Can you tell us, please, as part of the meals that you got, did you ever get vegetables or eggs or meat or dessert, something sweet?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No dessert, no. There was always meat. I don't know about fruit, whether there was or wasn't. I didn't pay any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How about vegetables or eggs?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Eggs, yes; vegetables, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Butter?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Butter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did you get your drinking water from while you were working?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: We brought our drinking water from home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many times a day the detainees, the people who were detained in the camp, ate?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps what they ate?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The same thing we ate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, when we received our -- the schedules for the food, for the meals, they would get their meals first and then we would get our food. The same platoon would take them food and us that same food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you see the food being actually taken by the platoon?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can see them taking the food and bringing the food to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what types of containers, if any, or how did they take the food? Can you describe the process physically?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It was a classical type of container, the type used in the army for food, and food was brought in containers of that kind, standard issue containers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how many trips did they have to make to take the food to feed the number of people who were detained?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: They came to us twice a day, once for one meal, the second time for the second meal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were they located closer to you? Were the people who prepared the food located physically closer to you or close to you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The same distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you -- perhaps you may have misunderstood my question a moment ago. There were a number of people, a fairly large number of people, in the camp, were there not?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. I couldn't see from that distance how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When the guards took what you thought was their food to them, how many guards did it take to take all the food? How many trucks? How many containers? If you can just give us a number. And maybe the type of containers. You mentioned classic containers. Were they containers for liquid? Help us a little bit to understand that.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: They were containers which were taken to us. For our purposes one container would be full of food, another container for bread, and a third container for tea. Now, quantity-wise, I would say the containers were about -- between 50 to 100 litres, of that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And do you know how many of those containers were taken to feed the people in the camp whenever their mealtime was?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you: Why did you bring your drinking water from home?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Because there wasn't any water where I was doing guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was no drinking water, water you could drink? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: There was no water at all. Where I was, there was no water at all. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I withdraw the objection. The witness has already answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Anyway, Mr. Simic, if you leave it to the witness, the witness will always answer, will give an answer himself. So perhaps rather than making frequent interruptions, we can let the witness answer for himself. So place your confidence in the witness, Mr. Simic. You see he's able to answer. Ms. Somers, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, did your shift in the second circle include working at night? I know you indicated people did work at night. Did you ever work at night?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you worked at night -- first of all, 500 to 600 metres was the estimate of the distance of your circle from the camp; is that right? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before I ask you the next question, I wonder if you might be willing -- if you don't mind getting up -- just to point something out. This is a model of the Omarska camp, a bit dusty, but a model. I wonder if you could take the pointer, the piece of metal that's in front of it, and show us, please, a couple of things. It will just take a minute. I hope it won't be inconvenient for you. Would you mind getting up and doing that? You'd have to leave your earphones, but -- thank you. Can you hear me okay now? Are your earphones working?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, if you'd help us, using this model of Omarska camp, can you indicate on which side of the camp you were assigned to guard duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're pointing to the area in front of the green strip on the model.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the assistance, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the record, it would be to the right of what has been described as the "white house." Is that correct? It was to the right of that "white house"? That was the area to which you pointed?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It depends on what side you're looking at it from, your angle of vision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From where you're standing, pointing to the right? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, yes? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness never mentioned the term "white house," and I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Simic. We are coming to a situation where interruptions are not welcome. It is true that Ms. Susan Somers is trying to -- doing her best to pinpoint the point described by the witness, and she said that it was to the right of the "white house," and that was the point that he indicated. Of course, we do know, Mr. Krstan Simic, that the witness did not mention the "white house." We all know that. But the witness pointed to a spot. Now, Ms. Somers had to describe that spot for us for the record. It is true that Ms. Somers is at one place in the courtroom and the witness is in another position, but we're all -- all of us here are following the proceedings. So there is the administration building, there's the canteen or restaurant, and in -- standing where the witness is standing, I would say, if I were asking him the question, I would say, "You mean after the restaurant or the canteen, in the direction of the "white house," to the right." I would say that myself. Now, it's up to Ms. Susan Somers to describe the location. And it's true, Mr. Simic, that the witness never mentioned the "white house," but if you attended the proceedings attentively, Ms. Susan Somers was trying to indicate the exact spot by describing it for purposes of the record, for the record. So let us not split hairs. Ms. Susan Somers, please continue with your knowledge of geography, north, south, east, west. So give us the orientation. You can orient yourself and then guide the witness as to direction. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Assuming that we're looking -- just for the sake of our conversation right now, with north being that way, the point -- would you repoint to the area where you were? That would be helpful. Would you do that one more time? Show us again where you worked. Show us again, please, with the pointer where you worked.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Based on what I had described as being north, it would be northeast of -- northeast of the green area, and the reference to the white building, it would be to the right of the white building. Is that a fair description, if you were talking to me and trying to show me now?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thanks very much. Did you change your posting, your location, in the second circle from time to time while you were on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were always at that first location that you showed us.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you can sit down, if the usher would be -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take advantage of this interruption, Ms. Susan Somers, to make a suggestion. There is a piece of paper with a diagram -- we have the diagram of the model in the courtroom. Perhaps it would be more practical for next time to prepare the diagram and show the diagram to the witness, and then he could indicate what you want him to indicate. Perhaps that would facilitate matters and speed them up. But it's up to you, of course. Please proceed, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. I was unaware of that, and I appreciate -- as you know, at this phase, it's very helpful for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, from the place where you showed us where you had guard duty, either during the day or during the night, whenever you were on duty, did you ever hear screams, screams of people?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From the location that you showed us, did you ever hear the sound of gunfire, of gunshots, of weapons being discharged, ever?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever observe trucks or any other vehicles leaving Omarska camp with dead bodies on them?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a specific vehicle. Did you ever see what is called a yellow TAM, or TAM, coming in or out or moving about Omarska? From the position where you were working, did you ever see that, a yellow TAM?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked by my counsel opposite about your military service in 1991. Now, you indicated you were originally with, was it, the 43rd Motorised Brigade; is that correct? The 43rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you also participate -- did you participate in combat in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever in the 5th Kozara Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When were you in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In which battalion or unit of that brigade were you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any awards or military medals or honours during the time you were in that Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I did not. I just got a prison term.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For what? What happened?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I wasn't good --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: -- a good guy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Avoidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of? Avoidance of what?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Avoidance of going to the battlefield, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long were you locked up?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: For a short period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is that? How long would that be?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Between seven and ten days. I was under investigation and then sent to the battlefield again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where were you kept when you were locked up? Where were you kept when you were locked up?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what type of facility? Where? The name of the place where you were kept. Was it a military camp, a prison? What was it?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: It was a military institution. It wasn't a prison or a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were sent to the battlefield again after you were released from Banja Luka, from the prison, where did you serve? Which battlefield were you on?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From what time period to what time period?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were locked up, how was the food in the prison?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Good, because you could bring in food from outside. So my brother and my sister would bring in food for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Also, I wanted to ask you about your weight. When you were working in the second circle, going back to that time period, how much did you weigh when you went into your work - I think it was June of 1992, you said - and how much did you weigh when you finished your work in August?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: When I started working, I weighed 89 kilos, and when I stopped working, 89 kilos. The same weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to jump - I'll only jump once - but when you were in Banja Luka in that short-term lock-up, were only soldiers kept there? And if so, were they only Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Only soldiers and, yes, only Serb soldiers; although, actually, there were some Muslim and Croat soldiers serving in our army who had committed an offence, misdemeanour, did not go to the battlefield when they should have, were late a day or two. And then the military police would take them into custody and put them there and then take them off to the battlefield afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you go in front of a judge before you were put in that lock-up?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Chamber, I think, should be given Exhibit -- it's from May 31st, 2/4.11. Exhibit 2/4.11, this is a document that Mr. Krstan Simic also had presented. It's the May 31st document that shows the setup of the Omarska camp. I know that everyone has it, but I want to make sure the Chamber gets a copy right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should, first of all, like to ask Ms. Somers to ascertain whether the witness has ever seen the document. The witness is a mechanic. In a similar situation, when I asked a witness to explain a document which was a very expert one, the Chamber told me that it was not up to the witness to explain a highly involved, legal document of the type shown him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Krstan Simic, let's see. I would like to draw Ms. Somers's attention to the time. Please don't overstep your time limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thanks very much. If the Chamber will let me know when I can respond, I will be glad to. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just bear that in mind, otherwise we're going to lose a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, I'd like you to just comment on a couple of points. One is you may or may not have seen this document, and your personally seeing it would not be terribly critical because it concerns the area in which you were working, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, either you're going to ask the witness, "Do you know the document, Witness?" and then go on with your question; but if you're asking a question without the document, then there's no need to place the document in front of the witness, then you can just go ahead with the question. You see what I mean. If the question is connected to the document, you must first ask whether the witness has seen the document and then go ahead with your question. If you're asking him the question without showing him the document, then we don't need the document shown him at all, we don't need the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I follow what you were saying. I was trying to approach it from a different angle. But I certainly will go back and lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
