utterances.text: The document you see in front of you, which is a document dated the 31st of May, 1992, coming from the public -- at the end of the document, there is a signature of Mr. Simo Drljaca. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any written rules and regulations that would have come down from above about the various roles of persons who had anything to do at all with the setting up or the functioning of Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know of any rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will discuss this with another witness, Your Honour. I think the question -- the particular question, although I'm confident he may know, I think it would be, perhaps, a bit difficult for him. Thank you, Mr. Pusac. I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Pusac, my learned friend has asked you about the position of your tent where you had guard duty within this so-called second ring. I would like to ask you to tell the Judges whether, between your tent and the Omarska centre, there were any obstacles or hills. Did you have a proper view of what was happening in Omarska? Could you clear that up in a few sentences, please?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we couldn't see much because we were 500 to 600 metres away. Also, there were shrubs and trees because, of course, we couldn't put up our guard post in a clearing. So we too had to conceal our position. And from there where we were, it was difficult to see anything at all. In fact, we saw nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: One additional question. So according to the rules, did you set up your tent in an area where it would be sheltered and concealed from others? So where you were, you also could not have a proper view of the camp?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think you told us that you understood the duty of yourself and others in the second circle to prevent the -- or to guard against the escape of prisoners out of the camp and the unauthorised or people who shouldn't be going into the camp going into the camp; is that right? I mean, you had to have some function. What did you understand the function of your position in the second circle? When you were on guard duty, what were you looking for? What were you watching out for when you were on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: At my guard post, I had to watch out for people coming from the outside and, of course, any people who might leave from the inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My next question then is: How were you or your fellow soldiers in the second circuit -- second circle, I'm sorry, how were you to know who was an authorised person to go into the camp or not? I mean, if you saw some people approaching the gate of the camp -- could you see the gate of the camp, the regular gate where trucks went in and out or where people might go in and out? Was that in view from your guard post? Could you see the regular gate where people would go in and out from where your guard post was?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, what were you guarding? I mean, I'm not quite clear then. If you couldn't see people who were coming in and out, what were you supposed to look for? No. I'm getting French. I can't hear the English. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Interpreters, can you check your microphones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If somebody will say something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's all right now. What were you looking for? If you were on guard and you couldn't see people coming to the gate or going out of the gate, where would you be looking? What would you be looking for?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The position of my guard post was not on that side, it was on the opposite side of the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So when you were -- according to your understanding then, you would be watching out for people who might be coming out of the camp who shouldn't -- or going into the camp who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shouldn't but not in the regular gates, over the -- on the other parts of the camp where there were no gates; is that right? You had to watch it for, as you said, people coming in and going out. So I'm just trying to ascertain, you know, what you were looking for, people who weren't going in and out the regular way? Might be sneaking out along the perimeter or along the part of the camp that you could see?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So to clarify this then, were you in a position to see any -- the trucks that brought in the food every day? When the food containers came in, were you in a position to see those trucks coming and going to the camp? The food trucks, the trucks that we talked about that had the containers of food.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No. Only the trucks that came to our -- to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What would be the trucks that came to you, just your own military trucks?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, what other kind of trucks would you see?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Privately-owned trucks, because they had been requisitioned, and they crossed through the fields and meadows to reach us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To reach you but not to go into the camp. The trucks that we're talking about now, did they go into the camp at any point or just to your tent, just to your guard post?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: They only came up to our guard post, and, of course, the other guard posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In the two months that you told us you were at this same guard post, did you, in fact, ever see anybody trying to get into the camp or trying to come out of the camp from your viewpoint of your guard post?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you never saw any unauthorised people trying to get in or come out?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: From your point of view -- I think I know the answer but I want to make sure. From your advantage point at the guard post, could you see any prisoners, just see them, not maybe close enough to recognise them, but just see bodies inside the camp? I don't mean dead bodies. I mean people walking around, prisoners. Could you see -- could you make out figures inside the camp from where your guard post was?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No. I could just see the roof of this building here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So you couldn't see where any of the clumps of people were inside the camp at all. So the whole two months you were there -- is this right or wrong: The whole two months you were there, you never actually saw a prisoner or an inmate of the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: You told us that from everything you knew, you were getting the same food as the inmates who were being served by the Quartermaster Platoon, right? I mean, they brought the containers of the food.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you have anyway of knowing whether you were getting the same quantities of food that the inmates were getting? If it was the same food? I'm just asking you if you had anyway of knowing - if you didn't, okay - whether or not the amount of food that you were getting was the same as, say, each inmate might be getting inside.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Pusac, could you tell us, what were the instructions that Zdravko Maric, for example, who was your superior, gave you to carry out? What were your instructions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: There can be no exits and no entries. For any other assignments, we will be duly informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Entry and exit from where and to where?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Leaving the compound, leaving the circle, and entering it from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation I received was "leaving that place." Which place?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You told me that your instructions were, "Prevent anyone from entering and prevent anyone from leaving." My question is: From entering where and leaving what? Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Entering from the outside and from leaving the circle, from going outside the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What circle?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Not in the literal sense the circle, but the compound where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. Why don't you use the proper word. When you say the "circle," you mean the Omarska centre. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your task was to prevent anyone from entering or leaving the Omarska centre.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the time that you were there - Judge Wald already mentioned the two-month period - did you ever see anything unusual or out of the ordinary in terms of security?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be right to say that things were going so well that if you hadn't been there, you wouldn't have been necessary?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have another question. How was the food transported?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: By trucks of private owners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you describe those trucks, what type of trucks they were?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: The brand was Zastava 750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The containers, were they small, individual containers or were these large containers where all the food was contained? You know, you can have a large container which are then divided up into small portions, or were they already served in the small portions?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: They were large containers, and we had our own small dishes, and then the food was poured from the big container to each of us individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. And when the food was in the trucks, could you see the food that was inside?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the receptacles were open or closed?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could you see then?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK PUSAC
utterances.text: When the food was being served out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Mr. Pusac, that brings to an end our questions. We thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher is going to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence now calls the last witness for this week. His name is Djordje Stupar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stupar. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness' other microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming. You will first be answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Krstan Simic, you have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You know that my name is Krstan Simic, and together with Mr. Lukic, we are representing Mr. Kvocka. So our questions will be relevant to the events that occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me ask you to make a pause after my question so that everything can be interpreted and to avoid any overlap for the benefit of the record and Their Honours, of course. Could you please, for the record, tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Djordje Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: On the 17th of December, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is that where you are residing?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Have you done your military service and where?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I have, from November 1993 until February 1995. No. I'm sorry. November 1973 until February 1975, in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was your speciality during your military training?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The platoon for maintenance, as a metalworker.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you completed your military service, were you registered as a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I was, under the same speciality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Will you make a pause after my question, please. Where were you registered as a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I do, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What did you do in the course of 1991 and 1992 in your civilian life?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I had a private business of my own that collected wastepaper and recycled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was your firm based?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your company, as assets, did you have a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had three trucks and a forklift.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: According to the regulations in force at the time, was it possible for the assets, such as private vehicles, to be requisitioned from private and legal entities for the need of military exercises or the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were any of your vehicles on the list for requisitioning should there be a mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. One truck was subject to requisitioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was the place of requisitioning?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The Rakovacke Bare locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is that locality? Is it the headquarters of a military unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I know there was a shooting ground there for military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In the course of the first half of 1992, was your vehicle, your truck, actually requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Franjo Gagula?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: He is an acquaintance of mine. He is a florist; he purchases and sells flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of his vehicles were requisitioned in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. A Nissan and a Golf 2, as we call it, a VW.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, according to the rules that were being enforced at the time, what were the rights of the owners of vehicles that were being requisitioned for the needs of a particular military unit, as envisaged by the mobilisation plan?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Owners had some rights of compensation. Whoever requisitioned the vehicle was under the obligation to return it to the owner in the same condition in which it was requisitioned, and our obligation was to give it in proper operational order.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the vehicle of Mr. Franjo Gagula?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: While the vehicle was being used for the purpose for which it was requisitioned, the vehicle disappeared, it was stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Gagula was given compensation for the loss of his vehicle, a Golf?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: He said that he was given a court ruling in his favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he tell you which court passed this decision?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think he said it was the Banja Luka Municipal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he ever actually collected the sum envisaged for compensation of this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think that until 15 days ago he did not collect the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Talking to you, did he tell you that that decision was final?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think he did say that it was final, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What ethnicity is Mr. Franjo Gagula?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: He is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, while you were engaged in your private business, were you well-off?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you own an apartment in Belgrade as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I have a brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Bosko Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where is your brother, Bosko Stupar, living?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: He is living in Toronto, Canada, ever since 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How old was your son in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: He was 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In 1992, as a military conscript, were you drafted?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: In 1992, I was first drafted to go to the Banja Luka airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In what status? In what position? What speciality, rather?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: As a metalworker.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether you were a member of the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The first time I was mobilised by the army; after that I was mobilised for the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you remember in what month you became a member of the reserve police force, which meant a change of your status?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, let us go back to these questions regarding mobilisation for a moment, because I omitted to ask you: As the owner of a vehicle or another technical asset which, under the regulations in force, came under requisitioning orders by a military unit or institution, if you were to ignore such an obligation, were any sanctions envisaged for failure to observe those regulations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. Criminal liability was envisaged. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to show members of the Trial Chamber ... [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There is no translation on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Interpreters, please check your buttons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we apologise. Counsel is distributing copies of the document to Their Honours, the Prosecution, and the Registry, which he will tender into evidence later on as D41/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, please go ahead. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were criminal charges filed with civilian or military courts for military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think it was to military courts. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness this document just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, the document you are showing, is it relevant to this witness or not? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] This document regards relevant facts we have discussed here, and it speaks to the fact that a certain vehicle was requisitioned. We don't even have to see it. The prosecution files criminal charges and certain sanctions are entailed. We only want the Trial Chamber to have a full picture of the state of affairs as it was then and that which was relevant to all persons that had a wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Simic. The problem is that this witness is not a lawyer. This document does not concern him directly, but I will allow this question. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, just one question. Is this the procedure which applied if anyone should refuse to hand over their vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Just another one. It says, "Request for Investigation Against Andja Jovic." What ethnicity is this person?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I would like to go back just for a moment and then we will pick up where we left off. What were your duties in your role as reserve policeman in the first half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: We physically provided security of the Banja Luka radio station, of the municipality of Banja Luka, of the government auditing agency, SDK, and we also did guard duty in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was your status identical to that of a regular, professional policeman, in terms of your duties?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did active-duty policemen provide security for these facilities together with you? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said that he is not personally aware who provided the security, so Mr. Simic is asking the question again. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a minute. You know that there is this delay because of interpretation. Mr. Simic, you may continue now. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just asked whether the status was identical, and my next question relates to facts, who did what, things that can be observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Together with you personally, did any of the professional policemen work there providing security?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, did you at one point, facing the problems created by prewar and then wartime conditions, decide to leave both the reserve police force and the town of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Counsel is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, please ask your question but rephrase it first. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did, together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, the living conditions weren't normal and I was fearing for the safety of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When did you make the decision to do this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Somewhere at the end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it an easy thing to do, just to decide and say, "Well, I'm leaving now"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, it was not that easy. It required time and preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Why was it difficult to do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, Banja Luka was in a very special situation. It was not possible to leave without special exit permits and permits for passage through the corridor was opened towards Serbia, the corridor you had to use if you wanted to leave, and from there on to other destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber from which date was this corridor opened? When did the physical connection between Belgrade and Banja Luka start to exist?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The 28th of June, 1992, the surface connection between Belgrade and Banja Luka came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Before that day, was there any traffic of people or goods from either direction?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No. Banja Luka, that is, the entire region, was surrounded, encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it a blockade of the region? How did foodstuffs, cigarettes, medicines, find their way into Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: All that was very difficult. There was no electricity, it was difficult to get food, there was no oxygen, newborn babies were dying due to banal problems, and everybody who lived there experienced the same conditions. The situation was very difficult for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, do you remember how much we paid for a sack of flour while we were surrounded?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot remember, because inflation was staggering even then, but it was a lot of money, dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long was there no electricity, the maximum period of time without electricity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I believe it was 42 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it a period of high temperatures?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. Heats were very bad. It was difficult to preserve food. You don't have the fridge; you can't use it. You have to cook on fire. It was 40 degrees outside and about the same inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: When you spoke of the difficulties involved in leaving for Belgrade on a private or a business trip, could you tell the Trial Chamber what did it look like exactly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, before I took my family there, I made the trip twice to check what it was like. I had regular civilian papers, but I was wearing my uniform to make it easier. It made it easier to pass. It was a trip of about 440 kilometres. I think 40 kilometres in two stages across zones of military actions. There was shelling on sections of the road. It was hard to make the decision to risk my wife's and my children's lives and take them there, but still I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, concerning that departure - I'm not speaking about you but about any person - was it necessary to get a permit to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. You had to get a permit for this trip, travel permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who issued it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were there any changes at any point, changes in the jurisdiction in terms of who issued these permits?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: All I could notice was that the place where these permits were issued changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where were they issued earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: At the police station at first, and then the office was transferred to a cabin of the local commune of Borik, I think one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you remember who signed such a travel permit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On the road from Banja Luka to Belgrade, that is, Bijeljina, because that was the point where you were leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina, did anyone check you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, travelling with my family to Belgrade, my son was making -- was keeping a record of the checkpoint we passed and there were 43 marks -- sorry, 64 marks on his record; that is, we passed 64 checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you stopped at each of these checkpoints? Did you have to show your papers and explain why you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Almost at each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did everyone at all times have the possibility to come to this station and ask for this permit, just saying, "I'm going to Belgrade," or did they have to explain and document their request?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Of course you had to provide documents. Of course everyone could ask for this permit, but not everyone could get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was the reason you cited for leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I said it was a business trip, required for my business purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you have gone there and said, "I'm sick and tired of this. I don't like this. Gentlemen, let me go. Let me have this permit"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No, you couldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you, in keeping with the regulations then in force, unlawfully leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, by means of deception?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you do it by deceiving the authorities, making them believe that the purpose of your trip was different from what it actually was?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: We can call it that. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Under the law and in practice, were there any consequences or sanctions envisaged for people who decided of their own accord to leave their military, their wartime assignment, or their work obligation assignment in whichever unit they were posted to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: They were subjected to prosecution as deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was such an act supported or condemned by the majority of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the communities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: It was supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was it supported generally that deserters should be prosecuted or not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: It was supported indeed that they should be prosecuted as deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you in a position to go to Belgrade with your family? Would you have been able to do that if you had not had that apartment or were you materially provided for? If you hadn't been materially provided for.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't think I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: From the 15th of September until the 26th of December, 1992. That means two months and nine or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What did you decide to do then?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I left the country and went to Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Because everything was starting to be felt in Belgrade as well. There were refugees, unemployment, insecurity. Those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: This decision to go to Canada together with your family, was it possible to accomplish because you had a brother there already who already had a family there and got settled?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: My brother provided me with the papers necessary for me to leave for Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that such actions were subject to prosecution, the filing of criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were any criminal charges filed against you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you aware that similar charges were filed against other persons?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Of course they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did a man named Arso work in those -- with you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he have an only son?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did his son work in 1991/1992, in which town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. He worked in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he too leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. In the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were criminal charges filed against him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And despite the danger you were aware of, the danger of prosecution, you made your decision as you did, right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity to hear about rulings made by military authorities against persons in your status?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point I would like to ask the usher's assistance in distributing to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution a set of verdicts brought by the Military Court of Banja Luka, and it would be marked D42/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, to inform the witness? The witness said that he never found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity to hear about rulings made by military authorities against persons in your status?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No. Why then this document, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one of the questions being asked and which will be asked during these proceedings was the question of choice or lack of choice in deciding to leave your place of residence. We only want this Trial Chamber to gain an insight into their situation and to realise that it was not possible to leave without the support that Mr. Stupar had and without the financial advantages such as the apartment in Belgrade. And the verdicts, which the Trial Chamber will see if they admit this into evidence, reflecting the entire system will realise what the relationships were at the time and what options were open to the people who are being -- who are on trial here. I think that is -- I would say that this is reason enough, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to these documents, Your Honour. As Your Honour said, this witness said very clearly and directly that he is totally unaware of any rulings which were made by any military high authorities. And also, I see no basis for Mr. Simic to enter these things because these, which I just see, the documents refer to many persons and with certain judgements, and the witness has not spoken anything about these documents, and he in fact very clearly said at the outset that he knows nothing about these verdicts. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask a question about your objection. Admittedly leaving this witness out who has said he doesn't know, do you have some inherent objection to documents like this coming in as exhibits simply to show that, you know, if they've been listed in exhibits that they're judgements of the Military Court of Banja Luka, showing that they prosecuted people who wouldn't -- who left while they were still on military status? I mean, is there anything inherit you object to apart from the lack of linkage with this particular witness? I think the purpose is pretty clear, what he wants. He wants to show that it was pretty hard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But Mr. Simic has not referred to the law, as to what law these judgements pertain to, under what circumstances it had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yours is an authentication objection or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, about the law, under which law which these people have been tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So in your judgement, what would he have to do? In your judgement, what would he have to do, bring in an expert in Banja Luka law or something and explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: At last some -- the Act itself, the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is it makes no sense to tender or admit -- I would say it makes no sense to show this document to the witness if he says he was never aware of them. Another -- there may be another way to tender these documents into evidence, but for this witness, they are not relevant. If you present these documents to the witness now, he will say what he already said, "I was not aware of them." That's the problem. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept your suggestion. It was not my intention for these documents to be related to Mr. Stupar, to be linked to Mr. Stupar alone. But Mr. Stupar says explicitly that anyone who violated the regulations or failed to hand in their vehicles was subject to prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to repeat the witness' testimony. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just another sentence, please. May I respond to Mr. Waidyaratne? The legislation underlying these judgements is the criminal law of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was in force from 1991 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. It was not switched on. I was saying, I just read that it was Article 214, Paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 226. That is something that we can read from the document. But I'm going to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, we agree that these documents have nothing to do with the witness. What is strange is that you are asking now for those documents to be tendered. They have nothing to do with the testimony. I think that they are a part of a whole set of documents that you mentioned in your prior brief, pre-Defence brief, and in relation to which the Chamber said that it would wait to see the documents in order to be able to decide whether or not the Chamber would admit them. We made such an announcement at the beginning of this week. I can't be more specific now and you know I am talking off the bat. But the arguments that you mentioned, documents under D59 until I don't know which number, you know that the Prosecution objected to some documents and not to others. We said at the beginning of this week that all those documents need to reach the Trial Chamber for us to be able to examine them and then make a decision. So my suggestion to you is to withdraw your request to admit these documents but to collect all the documents that you would like to tender into evidence, to have all those documents given to the Trial Chamber. We will review them - the Chamber already knows the opinion of the Prosecution - and then the Chamber will rule. Why don't we act in an organised manner? We have already made such a decision and that is why I reacted. I see no link between these documents and this particular witness. I can see that there is relevance for the case but not in this way. If you agree, please send to the Trial Chamber all the documents, the whole batch, the whole set of documents, that you told us you would like to tender into evidence - you told us this in your pre-trial brief - and the Chamber, as it said at the beginning of this week, will review them and decide whether or not to admit them. What is your response, Mr. Simic? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept your suggestion. I withdraw these documents. In the view of the Prosecution, these are the only documents where they have concern over their relevance. They are, for now, withdrawn and we will wait for another opportune moment to tender them, once you have made the decision regarding the relevance of these documents for the case. I thank you very much. That is all for now. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are returning the documents. Mr. Simic, we lost quite a bit of time because, in a certain sense, we have already made a decision. We communicated to the parties that the Chamber was waiting for you to send us the documents for us to be able to review them. In any event, we will decide. Because, in my opinion, I tend to feel that the documents speak for themselves. So if you send us the documents, they speak for themselves. We will analyse them - we already know the position of the Prosecution - and after that we will make our decision. So thank you very much. You said that you had finished your examination-in-chief, didn't you? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, then. It is five past one so we are going to have our long break now, that is, a long break of 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stupar, you're now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, and it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Mr. Waidyaratne who will be asking you questions. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stupar.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know any of these accused who are here in this court?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What made you come -- what made you come here to give evidence on behalf of Mr. Kvocka? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We discussed that at length, and we said that witnesses testify in the interests of justice, and this particular witness was called by the Defence of Mr. Kvocka to give his testimony and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Simic, who is appearing for Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, we know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, by sight, at least 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just want to know. Only by sight?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: That long, yes. And we greet each other -- we have been greeting each other and exchanging a few words for, let me say, the past 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did anybody contact you or was it on your own that you came to give this testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I was contacted by Mr. Simic in order to speak about how I left my native town and went to Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stupar, now, you said that you were mobilised before you went to Belgrade. It was not very clear. Could you kindly clear up as to when you were stationed in the Banja Luka airport?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: At the airport in Banja Luka, I was a drafted soldier at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then you said that you left to Belgrade at the end of July 1992; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I left for Belgrade with my family on the 15th of September, 1992. That was the last time. I definitely left for Belgrade on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You left Banja Luka in September.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The 15th of September, 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you still mobilised during that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So is it your position that you deserted?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was any action taken against you subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: As far as I know, the indictment is still open in the military department charging me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: -- and that I will be criminally prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you come back from Canada to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you given any charges for deserting after you came back?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can you say where is -- who charged you, which authority?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The ministry of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And it's still pending; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any other allegations or charges against you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stupar, you said it was difficult to leave Banja Luka in 1992, and in fact you had to go in your uniform for your own safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for my own safety and for me to be able to pass by more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that was the day when you started off in September. Now, you said that you had to get special permits, exit permits, and in fact you mentioned another permit, a travel permit. Could you tell me from where you get these permits? Was it difficult for you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: First of all, as a private individual, I open a travelling document in the name of my own company. On the basis of those travel certificates or documents, I go to a secretariat of some kind which then issues me with a permit for travelling to Serbia and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stupar, I'm talking about you leaving -- when you left Banja Luka in 1992, in the month of September; am I clear?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think you're clear on one point; that is to say, what I did was to open travel documents for my wife and for myself, and on the basis of those business travel documents, we were given permits, that is to say, my wife and myself. My children didn't need this kind of permit because they were minors, they were travelling with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you left under the pretext that you were going on a business trip; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, for any other individual, specially non-Serbs, do you know what they had to have to leave the country?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think that they had to have a lot of different papers, documents; that they had paid their electricity bills, that they had discontinued their telephone, that they had paid up all their utility dues and everything else. That was difficult to come by, because in order to get those documents, people would see that you were planning to leave. So I didn't dare do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is that it was very difficult for the non-Serbs to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Not only for non-Serbs, for everybody. It was more difficult, in fact, for Serbs to leave than for the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when the non-Serbs left, do you know what happened to their property? Especially I am speaking of -- referring to the landowners, like house and land?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. What I was bent on doing was getting me and my family out. That was my priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, what did you do to your assets when you left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I left them to a friend I could trust, for a certain amount of time, and I asked him to try and save those assets. We had reached an agreement that if he was faced with a difficult situation, that he was to leave everything. But he managed to safeguard my assets. I don't know how he managed to do that, but he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You did not have to turn them over to any authority, especially the authority which was in power during that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The very fact of handing my assets over, I would indicate to them that I was leaving the country and thereby bring myself and my family, and particularly my wife, who was a non-Serb, into danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stupar, I don't think you understood my question. You didn't have to turn over your assets, your house and property, to the Serbian authorities when you left? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has several times stated that he feigned a business trip. He wanted to cover the fact that he was leaving and, therefore, his assets and property were left to carry on working. As a Serb, he could not depart and say, "I'm leaving my assets and property." What he had to do was leave under the pretext of going on a business trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you tell us as to what happened to your house and property when you left Banja Luka? Did you have them when you returned in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's still mine. Everything is still mine, probably thanks to the fact that I didn't register that I was leaving. I didn't inform anybody that I was leaving. Had I done that, everything would probably have been confiscated and perhaps destroyed or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, if you're aware, do you know as to what the non-Serbs, especially the Muslims, who left Banja Luka had to do with their house and property?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you returned, did you see as to what happened to the Muslim houses and the property that they own?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, there's some people living in those houses and apartments, who were displaced from other areas, such as Sarajevo, Mostar, and so on, and they had suffered the same fate as those who fled from Banja Luka, perhaps even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And they are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stupar, if you know, do you know as to what the population was in 1991, the Muslim population in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that the majority of the Muslims left Banja Luka in 1992 or were forced to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in 1992 and 1993, they left Banja Luka. Most of the Muslims left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stupar, you spoke about, in your direct examination, about the difficult times that you had in Banja Luka. Were you, the Serbs, under threat in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You don't know any village or town which was attacked or was under threat in Banja Luka? No Serb towns were attacked? No villages were attacked?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, there was tension, war tensions. There was information put out and this raised tensions. Now, what was true in all this and what was said, I don't know. Perhaps we'll learn the truth one day. But we all lived the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: But you're unaware of any attacks of any Serb villages in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, there were some attacks around Mrkonjic Grad and villages thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stupar, just being in Banja Luka, were you aware, before your departure in 1992, that there were two mosques in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that, those buildings, the premises?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The Catholic church exists to the present day, both Catholic churches, whereas the two mosques that you are probably referring to were destroyed. Now, who the perpetrators were is not known to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You were talking about the requisition of the vehicles during the time of the conflict, and you said that some were compensated. Did you get any compensation for your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you make an application for compensation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why didn't you get compensation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you try to find out about it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you get to know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: They told me that I should let it be for the time being and not to take any steps in that direction. I was told that unofficially by some friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you are unable to give the reason as to why you were said so. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, just one more matter. The time that you left for Belgrade from Banja Luka, were you able to take any amount of money, currency exchange?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I had it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Unofficially.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know how much, officially, you could take out when you left the country?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How much money did you have when you left the country? Are you in a position to say that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: When I left Banja Luka, I had about 50.000 German marks, and two days after my departure from Banja Luka, I sent a truck to Belgrade which I then sold there for 35.000 German marks, which means that in Belgrade, I had a total of 85.000 German marks at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: But you know that it was not officially allowed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If you would bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, concluding, have you been by anyone promised any pardon, amnesty, or special treatment relating to the indictment that is pending against you for testifying today?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just have two basic questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, a little while ago, Mr. Waidyaratne asked you whether you received compensation for the vehicle that was requisitioned, and I'd now like to ask you to tell the Court whether your vehicle was returned to you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What application for compensation did you file?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: For anything out of order to be repaired, and there was some compensation for the daily use of my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was that a significant sum, the compensation that you received? And were there any major repairs to be done?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: The repairs were paid for by the army in 1992, when the vehicle was returned. And compensation for the days the car was used, I think that when this was paid out, it was a substantial sum. But as there was such rampant inflation at the time, the sum would be absurdly small, negligible, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned colleague also asked you whether you were promised any kind of amnesty or pardon with respect to your desertion and the charges brought against you, and in that connection, I should like to ask you the following: Are you aware, do you know that under pressure of the International Community and in keeping with the Dayton Accords, a law was enacted whereby all persons were amnestied in the territory of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina for this type of criminal action, criminal offences, of the kind that you were charged with?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does that mean that, in keeping with that law on amnesty, you are no longer the subject of prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a document of any kind stipulating that, pursuant to the amnesty law, you will not be further charged?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: No, I did not receive that. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Judge Fouad Riad, would you like to ask anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, just one question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Stupar, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Simic just asked you the question I wanted to ask, but I would like to have, perhaps a more, what can I say, fulfilling answer. You said you might have been amnestied or pardoned, but you were -- in fact, you went after that home and nobody mentioned to you that you were amnestied or pardoned; is that right? It's an important issue. Did you give it your attention and try to find out? Did they come to you and try to -- it's a very serious charge, desertion. Did you give it any follow-up or attention to know what's happened?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Those are two -- well, two points. Nobody came to inform me that I was amnestied nor that the charges brought against me had been stopped, nor did I ask to see what was happening with the file. So that it is -- they are frozen. They have not been solved. I don't know. They are frozen at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you know that they were frozen when you went back home, and you were going safely, knowing that nothing would happen to you with charges?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I assumed that everything would be all right and that nobody would touch me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald has no questions. I have one. Perhaps it's my fault, but I didn't quite understand, what was the date of your return to Banja Luka from Canada? I think it was 1998.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you remember the date with greater precision, the exact date?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I think it was the middle of September 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answer to a question from Mr. Simic, you said that you were aware of the amnesty law. Do you know the date of that law?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I do not. I think it was part of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you another question. Before returning to Banja Luka or Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you know, were you aware of this law on a general amnesty?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I was. I knew that it existed. Now, whether it was being implemented fully is something I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that charges against you were still valid. What does that mean, that they were still pending?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: What I meant was that in a dispute over my apartment in August, they showed me at a court hearing a document saying that criminal proceedings were under way in the Defence Ministry against me because I had illegally left the country in 1992/1993, because the authorities couldn't establish exactly when it was I had left the country. So that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date that you mentioned, August, that's August 2000, or what year was that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes, August 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So these charges, were they covered by the amnesty?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Perhaps there will be -- I would have a good solution, but I have no right to tell you that, I realise that. I have no further questions for you. All that remains for me to say is to thank you for coming and to wish you a safe return home. Thank you very much. I will ask the usher to accompany you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Simic, no more witnesses for today? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour, no more witnesses. We have managed to abide by the time. I hope my guess will be as right for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope for even more than that, that we will be able to make even more progress. I do congratulate you that you have fulfilled your programme, but I do wish us to speed things up as much as possible. I think I understand that Ms. Susan Somers has something to say to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are two matters. One is, I think, appropriate for open session and it just concerns a request that if there -- if we could please have a confirmed order of witnesses from Mr. Simic by tomorrow so that we can make sure that we have everything in order to facilitate the presentation. The second matter, I think, would require about one minute of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us address those matters in that order. Mr. Krstan Simic, you heard what Ms. Susan Somers has just requested of you. Do you have anything to give her in response? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I will do that. The order of witnesses will be in accordance with the order notified in our brief with the exception of these seven witnesses. But, Your Honours, in view of the number of witnesses and the contents of their testimony, it may happen that the list will be reduced by three or possibly four witnesses. But we will inform the Prosecution in due time. In any event, the order will be identical to the one given in our last submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would be possible just to confirm. Does that mean the original brief, the 65 ter original brief, or the corrections? That's one part of the question. The second is: We have asked the Registry as to whether or not any aspect of the videolink preparation has been put in motion, simply because it does take time. And if any of these witnesses are going to be videolink witnesses, we just wanted to make sure the Chamber was apprised of the status of the technical side of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, can you clarify this point for Ms. Somers? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My answer is that Ms. Somers will receive a confirmed list tomorrow, and it is the same as the list that we submitted at our meetings. As regards the Defence for Mr. Kvocka, we have not envisaged any video witnesses unless there may be requests for the cross-examination of witnesses who submitted affidavits, and, of course, if the Trial Chamber grants those requests as that is within the competence of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I simply respond? We have filed a response to two affidavit witnesses, and we are seeking cross-examination as to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, you have already communicated that to the Chamber, have you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to take a step back. I thought it had been filed. It is to be filed before 4.00, but we are interposing objections to the admission. However, if the Chamber does admit, then we would ask simply for the right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are several things to address here. There are things that the parties can discuss amongst themselves and spare the Chamber, because we have established a rule for the parties to get in touch and try and reach agreement. If not, only then come to the Chamber. It is also quite possible for the Chamber to have to decide on certain matters, and this question you have raised on video testimony depends on the Chamber knowing first whether you wish to cross-examine or not the witness, whether you accept or not the affidavits, and so on. That depends. We don't know which affidavits you are not contesting and which you are. So there is no point in making a programme and sending people to Banja Luka unless you need them. We need to know what our needs are and make a programme accordingly. So tell us, please. Give us the information so that we can organise ourselves. When I say "tell us," I'm addressing myself to the Prosecution and also possibly the Defence, if they also have something to convey to us. So that is my response, Ms. Susan Somers. I think there is always a possibility to get in touch with Ms. MacIntosh or Mr. Olivier Fourmy so that we can organise things. I think that the Registrar will also take initiatives which are requested of it by the Chamber. They can't do anything without instructions from the Chamber. So we have a scheme within which each one must do his bit to reach our goal. I'm going to ask Mr. Krstan Simic for us to be able to decide about all the exhibits that you mentioned in your pre-Defence brief, to have those documents reach us and the Prosecution so that we can review them and see whether we will admit them or not. That is something that I have already said today. I think we have nothing else to deal with. Do you have something to tell us or to add before we adjourn for today? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we filed a request for protective measures yesterday, and we hope a decision will be forthcoming as the second group of witnesses are already coming tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the good news. The Trial Chamber has already taken a decision. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to ask if we could have a moment of private session. It's a matter that Mr. O'Sullivan and I wanted to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was just about to forget that. So we'll go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that Mr. Fila had something to say. You have the floor, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought this problem of videolink would be solved, but there are two issues that arise.
